name: Banxia Xiexin decoction (Hangeshashinto)
short: Japanese Kampo version, Hangeshashinto: an article links it to drug-induced liver injury (no case details given); 1 case report of pneumonitis. Decoction trials: sparse safety reporting.
text: Banxia Xiexin decoction (Ban-Xia-Xie-Xin-Tang) is the same named formula as the Japanese Kampo preparation Hangeshashinto (also written Hange-shashin-to or Hangeshashin-to), which is also used as a gargle for mouth inflammation (stomatitis); two cited reports concern that Japanese preparation. A 2025 article titled as reporting drug-induced liver injury associated with exposure to Hangeshashinto advises primary care physicians to be aware of the risk of drug-induced liver injury in patients prescribed Kampo medicines containing Scutellariae radix, such as Hangeshashinto, and to monitor them closely; its one-sentence abstract does not describe any patient, outcome or how the medicine was taken. A 1996 case report described a 72-year-old woman admitted with breathlessness and abnormal shadows on a chest X-ray, diagnosed with pneumonitis (lung inflammation) induced by Hangeshashin-to: all her drug treatment was stopped, her symptoms were relieved and her X-ray findings improved markedly; a white-cell (leukocyte migration inhibition) test was positive for both Hangeshashin-to and Byakkokaninjin-to (the abstract does not say whether she was taking the second preparation), and a lymphocyte stimulation test was positive for Hange, an ingredient of Hangeshashin-to; the abstract does not say how the medicine was taken. Safety reporting in trials of the decoction is sparse. In a 2013 systematic review of 16 randomized trials (1,302 patients) of the decoction or modified versions for diabetic gastroparesis, only one trial recorded adverse events, and no obvious adverse event occurred; the authors say the trials were of generally low methodological quality and that long-term safety is still uncertain. A 2023 meta-analysis of 57 randomized trials (5,525 participants) in functional dyspepsia reported fewer adverse events with the decoction, alone or with Western medicine, than with Western medicine or placebo, and a 2017 review of 12 trials of a modified version for reflux disease found adverse reactions no different from control groups; neither abstract gives event numbers or names the events. In a 2026 multicentre placebo-controlled trial in 129 people with advanced colorectal cancer, all also on chemotherapy and targeted therapy, a modified version given as granules for six months had no severe adverse events reported. The abstracts name Scutellariae radix and Hange as ingredients of Hangeshashinto but do not give the formula's full herb list. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
